proposal.problem: The shop tracks its stock and sales in Excel sheets together with a physical notebook for quick daily notes. Sales written in the notebook during the day must be copied into Excel later, so the two often do not match and the real stock level is never certain. When a popular product runs out, the owner usually notices only when a customer asks for it, so the sale is lost. Reordering is based on looking at the shelves rather than on data, which leads both to empty shelves and to products that stay unsold. The shop sells around 25 to 35 different products, and the owner spends about 4 to 5 hours every week counting stock, copying notes into Excel and checking sales (owner's answers by WhatsApp, 17 October 2026). There is no weekly report that shows which products sell best. The shop needs one simple tool that staff can use from a phone at the counter, that updates stock automatically with every sale, and that warns before a product runs out.
proposal.mission: ShopTrack gives the shop owner and shop staff of a small shop in Taif a simple Python web application to record sales, see live stock levels and receive low-stock alerts, so the shop owner stops losing sales to empty shelves and spends minutes, not hours, on weekly stock and sales reports.
proposal.outcome: Once ShopTrack exists, the shop owner opens one page and sees what is in stock, what sold this week and which products must be reordered today. Shop staff record a sale in a few taps on a phone, and the stock updates automatically, which the Excel sheets and notebook can never do.

entities.def: An item the shop sells, with name, category, barcode (optional), price and reorder level.
A change in the quantity of a product: stock in from a supplier, a sale, or a correction.
One sale recorded by staff: products, quantities, total and time.
A person who signs in: the shop owner (all rights) or a staff member (sales and stock-in only).

proposal.techWhy: schema.org gives standard terms for the shop's data (schema:Product, schema:Offer, schema:Order), so we do not invent our own names. JSON-LD lets ShopTrack export the product list in a form other tools and websites understand, while it stays ordinary JSON. RDFLib builds and reads that graph in Python. SHACL shapes, checked with pySHACL, validate every product imported from the shop's CSV (name present, price positive, stock a whole number) before it enters the database, so bad rows are reported instead of silently breaking the stock figures.

goals.goal: The shop owner always knows what is in stock and what to reorder, without counting shelves
goals.why: This is the change the mission promises.

proposal.spec: The shop owner signs in and imports the existing product list from a CSV file; each row is checked against a SHACL shape and invalid rows are listed with the reason. Owner and staff can add and edit products and register stock arriving from suppliers. Staff record a sale by choosing products and quantities; the system saves the sale, reduces the stock of each product and refuses a sale larger than the stock. When a product's stock falls to its reorder level, it appears in the low-stock alert list. The dashboard shows this week's sales total, a daily sales chart and the best-selling products. The owner can export products and sales as CSV or JSON-LD.

scenarios.text: Given a product with 10 in stock, when staff record a sale of 3, then the sale is saved and the stock shows 7.
Given a product with 2 in stock, when staff try to record a sale of 5, then the sale is refused with the message Not enough stock and nothing changes.
Given a CSV row with a negative price, when the owner imports the file, then that row is rejected and shown in the error report with its line number.
Given a product with reorder level 5 and stock 6, when one unit is sold, then the product appears in the low-stock alerts.
Given no sales recorded this week, when the owner opens the dashboard, then it shows zero sales and a clear empty-state message instead of an error.

proposal.useCase: Actors: Shop owner, Shop staff. Use cases: Import products (owner), Manage products (owner), Register stock-in (owner, staff), Record sale (staff, owner), View dashboard and alerts (owner), Export data (owner), Manage users (owner).

proposal.activity: Recording a sale: 1. Staff opens the sales page. 2. Searches or scans a product and enters the quantity. 3. System checks stock: if the quantity is larger than the stock, show Not enough stock and return to step 2; otherwise continue. 4. Staff confirms the sale. 5. System saves the sale and a stock movement and reduces stock. 6. If the new stock is at or below the reorder level, add the product to the low-stock alerts. 7. Show the sale receipt on screen. Import branch: owner uploads CSV, each row is validated, valid rows are saved, invalid rows go to the error report.
proposal.sequence: Staff -> Sales page: choose product and quantity. Sales page -> Flask route /sales: POST sale. Route -> SaleService: record_sale(items). SaleService -> Product repository: get stock. Product repository -> SaleService: current stock. SaleService -> Database: save Sale and StockMovement, update stock (one transaction). SaleService -> AlertService: check_reorder(product). AlertService -> SaleService: alert or none. SaleService -> Route: result. Route -> Staff: confirmation page with new stock.

proposal.classModel: Product (id, name, category, barcode, price, stock, reorder_level; methods: add_stock(qty), remove_stock(qty), needs_reorder()). StockMovement (id, product, quantity, kind: IN | SALE | CORRECTION, time). Sale (id, time, user, total; has 1..* SaleItem). SaleItem (product, quantity, unit_price). User (id, name, role: OWNER | STAFF, password_hash). Services: SaleService (record_sale), ImportService (import_csv, validate_row), ReportService (weekly_total, best_sellers, low_stock). Product 1 -- 0..* StockMovement; Sale 1 -- 1..* SaleItem; SaleItem * -- 1 Product.

proposal.model_Data: Tables: products, stock_movements, sales, sale_items, users in SQLite through SQLAlchemy. Stock is always changed through a stock movement inside one transaction, so stock = sum of movements and can be rebuilt. Constraint: stock >= 0.
proposal.model_Interaction: Sale sequence: Staff selects products -> page sends POST /sales -> SaleService checks stock for every item -> if all available, saves Sale, SaleItems and StockMovements in one transaction -> AlertService checks reorder levels -> page shows confirmation; if any item is short, nothing is saved and the short items are shown.
proposal.model_User_interface: Screens: 1) Sign in; 2) Dashboard (weekly total, daily chart, top 5, low-stock alerts); 3) Products list with search; 4) Product form; 5) Sales page with large buttons for phone use; 6) Import page with error report; 7) Export page.
proposal.model_Architecture: Layers: Flask routes and Jinja templates (presentation) -> service classes SaleService, ImportService, ReportService (business logic) -> repository classes over SQLAlchemy and SQLite (data). Validation module uses RDFLib + pySHACL on imported rows. Charts made with matplotlib and served as images.
proposal.model_Security: States of a user session: Signed out -> Signed in as Staff (sales, stock-in only) or Signed in as Owner (everything). Any request to an owner-only page from a staff session is refused (403). Passwords stored only as hashes (werkzeug.security).
proposal.libraries: Python libraries: Flask (web app and routing), SQLAlchemy with SQLite (database), pandas (reading CSV and Excel, weekly sales calculations), matplotlib (sales charts), RDFLib and pySHACL (JSON-LD export and validation of imported products), werkzeug.security (password hashing), and pytest (unit tests). Course topics applied: object-oriented programming with classes, inheritance and encapsulation (Product, Sale, User, service and repository classes), modules and packages, exception handling (NotEnoughStockError, invalid CSV rows), file I/O for CSV and JSON, decorators (login_required, role checks, timing), generators for reading large CSV files row by row, and automated unit testing with pytest.

risks.risk: The shop's existing product list is messy or incomplete
risks.mitigation: CSV import with validation and an error report; fix rows together with the owner.

risks.risk: The shop is in Taif, Saudi Arabia, so testing and feedback happen remotely
risks.mitigation: Host the app online, run the trial over a video call, and collect feedback by WhatsApp.

risks.risk: Free hosting is slow or goes down
risks.mitigation: Run locally on the owner's laptop as backup; keep a database backup.
